talks.title: Can you hear me now DEF CON
talks.teaser: RF communications using commodity SDR hardware for secure backchannel communications in security research.
talks.summary:
### Practical Sub-Gigahertz and Proprietary RF Operations
At 00:00, wireless security researcher Wasabi opens a practical field guide at the Wireless Village, exploring reconnaissance and offensive operations across sub-gigahertz and proprietary non-Wi-Fi radio spectrums.

### SDR Hardware Selection for Field Engagements
At 07:01, Wasabi evaluates software-defined radio (SDR) platforms for field portability. He compares devices like the RTL-SDR, HackRF One, and Yard Stick One, examining antenna selection, frequency ranges, and power management constraints during mobile operations.

### RF Range Benchmarking Across Urban Environments
At 14:02, the speaker presents empirical signal propagation testing. Evaluating 315 MHz, 433 MHz, and 915 MHz transceivers, he illustrates how lower frequencies penetrate reinforced concrete walls and urban structures far more effectively than standard 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi.

### Low-Power IoT and Telemetry Protocol Analysis
At 21:00, the presentation examines industrial wireless protocols, including LoRa, Sigfox, and proprietary smart metering standards. Wasabi details how these architectures achieve multi-kilometer range with minimal power consumption (10-20mA receive), making them ideal for covert telemetry.

### Mesh Relaying and Covert Field Deployments
Concluding between 28:01 and 35:01, Wasabi demonstrates mesh relay tactics. Compromising an intermediate ZigBee or sub-GHz node allows red teams to hop communications across physical perimeters, and he provides guidelines for weatherproofing autonomous, solar-recharged RF listening posts.

talks.title: Hunting Rogue APs Hard Lessons
talks.teaser: Given the challenge of locating a static Access Point this presentation highlights our strategy, pitfalls, and success.
talks.summary:
### Operational Lessons from Hunting Rogue Transmitters
At 00:00, security researcher t0ddpar0dy delivers a practical guide to locating unauthorized wireless access points and rogue transmitters in complex enterprise facilities at the Wireless Village. The speaker recounts field challenges encountered during real-world physical fox-hunting operations.

### Building Field Direction-Finding Equipment
At 07:30, t0ddpar0dy details the construction of portable direction-finding rigs. Utilizing a Raspberry Pi, USB Wi-Fi adapters supporting monitor mode, directional yagi antennas, and custom signal-strength logging scripts, researchers can measure received signal strength indicators (RSSI) while walking campus perimeters.

### Multipath Interference and Indoor RF Propagation
At 15:24, the presentation explores radio frequency propagation pitfalls inside commercial real estate. Concrete construction, elevator shafts, metallic HVAC ducting, and reflective glass windows distort RF signal paths, causing directional antennas to register false signal peaks that mislead search teams.

### Systematically Tracking Across Vertical Space
Concluding between 22:39 and 28:00, t0ddpar0dy shares strategies for hunting across multi-story buildings. He outlines methodical floor-by-floor search grids and triangulation techniques that help defenders locate rogue devices concealed above drop ceilings, inside wiring closets, or hidden within remote conference rooms.

talks.title: Attacking Gotenna Networks
talks.teaser: Talk will focus on privacy (or lack thereof) of gotenna networks. We will cover traditional attacks which have only been available to state sponsored prior to popularization and wide availability of software defined r...
talks.summary:
### Security Architecture of Off-Grid Mesh Devices
At 00:00, Vlad (Recompiler) presents vulnerability research targeting goTenna mesh radio devices, which enable off-grid text messaging and GPS sharing over VHF/UHF frequencies when cellular networks are unavailable.

### Decentralized Mesh Routing and APRS Tracking
At 04:02, the speaker explains the operational workflow of mobile mesh communications. Pairing with smartphones via Bluetooth Low Energy, goTenna units form ad-hoc multi-hop mesh networks, utilizing Automatic Packet Reporting System (APRS) protocols for emergency location beacons.

### Mobile App Cryptographic Key Storage Weaknesses
At 08:00, Vlad exposes implementation flaws in the goTenna mobile companion software. Reverse-engineering the application revealed that private encryption keys and device identity tokens were stored in unencrypted local application storage, allowing extraction and device impersonation.

### Protocol Fuzzing and Denial-of-Service
At 12:03 and 16:00, the presentation details protocol fuzzing methodologies. By broadcasting malformed packets over radio frequencies, researchers identified memory corruption bugs that caused unhandled exceptions in neighboring nodes, effectively disabling localized emergency communications.

### Identity Spoofing in Offline Environments
Concluding at 20:05, Vlad highlights the challenge of trust in offline environments. Without a central certificate authority to validate identities, adversaries can broadcast spoofed GID identifiers, impersonating trusted contacts or injecting deceptive location coordinates across decentralized mesh networks.

talks.title: RFNoC Accelerating The Spectrum with the FPGA
talks.teaser: RFNoC—FPGA-accelerated software-defined radio for high-performance spectrum analysis and wireless attacks.
talks.summary:
### Overcoming Host Processing Limits in Software-Defined Radio
At 00:00, Neel Pandeya and Nate Temple from Ettus Research introduce RFNoC (RF Network-on-Chip), an open-source FPGA processing architecture for USRP software-defined radios at the Wireless Village. The speakers address the bandwidth limits of traditional host-based SDR architectures.

### The Host CPU Bottleneck in Wideband Signal Processing
At 06:45, the presenters explain the computational bottleneck of streaming raw in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) samples over USB or Gigabit Ethernet to host CPUs. Processing multi-channel wideband spectrum strains host memory buses and CPU cache, frequently causing buffer overruns and dropped samples.

### Modular FPGA DSP Blocks and Direct Synthesis
At 13:12, Pandeya and Temple detail the modular architecture of RFNoC. The framework allows developers to implement digital signal processing (DSP) algorithms—such as Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs), digital down-converters (DDCs), and FIR filters—directly within FPGA logic using Vivado HLS or Verilog.

### High-Throughput Cellular Demodulation in Hardware
At 20:01, the speakers demonstrate real-time hardware signal processing. By chaining FPGA blocks together, they demonstrate high-speed multichannel WCDMA and LTE spectrum analysis executed entirely on-device at full analog-to-digital converter rates without burdening host compute resources.

### Seamless GNU Radio Integration
Concluding between 24:00 and 28:21, the presenters explain how RFNoC integrates with GNU Radio flowgraphs. Developers can control on-chip FPGA blocks using standard graphical blocks, combining FPGA acceleration with software prototyping flexibility.

talks.title: Its not wifi stories in wireless RE
talks.teaser: Wireless reverse engineering of non-WiFi protocols—SDR-based reconnaissance and security analysis.
talks.summary:
### Reverse Engineering Proprietary Wireless Protocols
At 00:00, hardware researchers Russ Handorf and Dominic Spill present war stories and systematic reverse engineering methodologies for analyzing unknown, non-Wi-Fi radio frequency transmissions.

### Signal Identification and Spectrum Analysis
At 11:00, the speakers walk through initial signal reconnaissance using SDR hardware (such as HackRF and USRP). They demonstrate capturing raw I/Q samples and analyzing visual waterfalls in tools like Baudline and Inspectrum to identify transmission characteristics without vendor documentation.

### Determining Modulation Schemes and Symbol Rates
At 22:00, Handorf and Spill explain how to extract digital data from analog waveforms. They detail identifying carrier frequencies, bandwidth limits, and modulation schemes—including Frequency Shift Keying (FSK), Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK), and Phase Shift Keying (PSK).

### Packet Framing, Demodulation, and Clock Recovery
At 33:01, the discussion turns to digital signal reconstruction. Using clock recovery and slicing algorithms, the presenters convert raw waveforms into binary streams, locating preamble synchronization words and reverse-engineering proprietary packet framing structures.

### Field Investigations and Automated Analysis Pipelines
Concluding between 44:01 and 55:02, the authors share field case studies, including decoding unknown neighborhood telemetry devices and reverse-engineering smart meter transmissions. They conclude by demonstrating automated signal analysis pipelines integrating GNU Radio flowgraphs with Wireshark protocol dissectors.

talks.title: Exploring the 802 15 4 Attack Surface
talks.teaser: Exploring 802.15.4 attack surface—Zigbee and low-power wireless protocol vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
### The Attack Surface of Low-Rate Wireless Networks
At 00:00, security researcher Ed (Faz) explores vulnerabilities across IEEE 802.15.4 wireless networks at the Wireless Village. Faz discusses the attack surface of low-rate personal area networks powering smart building automation, industrial sensors, and mesh ecosystems.

### Threat Categories in 802.15.4 Deployments
At 05:03, the presentation breaks down standard threat vectors affecting 802.15.4 implementations, including Zigbee, 6LoWPAN, and WirelessHART. Faz details how unencrypted or poorly authenticated sensor links remain vulnerable to packet eavesdropping, message replay attacks, node impersonation, and physical-layer RF jamming.

### Urban Reconnaissance and Wardriving in Sydney
At 09:52, Faz shares findings from wireless reconnaissance conducted across central Sydney, Australia. Walking urban corridors with portable sniffing gear, he discovered commercial building climate systems, smart power meters, and rooftop industrial sensors broadcasting cleartext 802.15.4 traffic.

### Intercepting Sensitive Infrastructure Telemetry
At 14:50, the speaker details analyzing captured frames near government and commercial facilities. Many detected sensor nodes utilized default pre-shared manufacturer keys, exposing diagnostic parameters, sensor states, and building control routines to unauthorized passive observation.

### Recommendations for Securing Sensor Meshes
Concluding between 18:00 and 20:02, Faz emphasizes defensive countermeasures for IoT network engineers. He recommends implementing robust application-layer encryption, disabling insecure over-the-air commissioning modes, and enforcing cryptographic key rotation across mesh deployments.

talks.title: SDR Basics Class
talks.summary:
### Foundations of Software-Defined Radio and DSP
At 00:00, SDR pioneer Balint Seeber delivers an intensive technical masterclass exploring digital signal processing (DSP) principles and practical Software-Defined Radio workflows.

### Sampling Rates, Nyquist Limits, and I/Q Data Streams
At 11:00, Seeber breaks down the mathematical foundations of RF capture. He explains complex baseband I/Q sampling, the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, and strategies for managing high-bandwidth data streams (50+ MSPS) using RAM disks to prevent packet loss.

### Building GNU Radio Flowgraphs
At 22:00, the instructor demonstrates building modular flowgraphs in GNU Radio Companion. He walks through integrating SDR source blocks, configuring finite impulse response (FIR) low-pass filters, and implementing frequency translators to extract individual channel audio from wideband RF recordings.

### Doppler Correction and Dynamic Calibration
At 33:01, Seeber examines advanced signal correction scripts. He illustrates using custom tools to correct phase offsets, compensate for oscillator frequency drift in inexpensive SDR dongles, and automate Doppler shift tracking for orbiting satellite passes.

### Real-Time Flowgraph Control via XML-RPC
Concluding between 44:00 and 55:02, Seeber showcases dynamic control architectures. By embedding XML-RPC server interfaces into GNU Radio flowgraphs, external Python scripts and web applications can dynamically retune frequencies, adjust filter bandwidths, and capture frames over network sockets in real time.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Goodwatch Update
talks.teaser: Travis Goodspeed provides an update on the Goodwatch open-source wrist-worn RF radio hacking and packet manipulation platform.
talks.summary:
### Open-Source Hardware Hacking on Wristwear
At 00:00, hardware hacker Travis Goodspeed delivers an entertaining update on the GoodWatch project at the Wireless Village. Goodspeed introduces the project as an open-source, programmable wristwatch engineered inside a classic Casio CA-53W calculator watch housing.

### Hardware Architecture: Texas Instruments CC430
At 07:43, Goodspeed describes the internal hardware retrofitting. By designing a custom replacement printed circuit board (PCB) powered by a Texas Instruments CC430 microcontroller, the watch combines an MSP430 processor core with an integrated Sub-1 GHz RF transceiver while utilizing the original LCD and keypad.

### Modular C Application Architecture
At 15:51, the presentation explores the firmware architecture. Goodspeed explains that watch features—ranging from countdown timers and world clocks to packet sniffers—are structured as independent modular C applications, allowing hobbyists to develop custom firmware modules.

### Sub-GHz Wireless Manipulation from the Wrist
At 23:54, Goodspeed demonstrates the wireless capabilities of the watch. Using the 16-key calculator keypad, he demonstrates capturing, demodulating, and transmitting Sub-GHz radio packets (around 315 and 433 MHz), triggering remote wireless relays and testing paging network protocols directly from his wrist.

### Community Contributions and Open Hardware Tradition
Concluding between 30:00 and 33:02, Goodspeed reviews open-source schematics, manufacturing tips for soldering miniature components, and highlights ongoing community contributions expanding the GoodWatch platform.
